**The Magistrate's Third Wife**

The rain had not ceased for seven days when Magistrate Chen arrived at his new post in Willow Creek Prefecture. The sedan chair bearers set him down before a mansion whose red gates had faded to the color of dried blood, and whose stone lions wore moss like funeral shrouds.

"Honored Magistrate," his elderly secretary whispered, "perhaps we should seek lodging at the inn—"

"Nonsense." Chen stepped into the puddles without care. "This is the official residence. We stay here."

The servants who greeted them were few and kept their eyes downcast. They led Chen through courtyards where weeds grew between cracked paving stones, past a garden pond choked with lotus leaves that had turned black. The air smelled of rot and old incense.

That first night, Chen heard the crying.

It came from the western wing of the compound, a woman's voice raised in the most pitiful weeping. Chen rose from his bed, lit a lantern, and followed the sound through empty corridors. But when he reached the western wing, he found only dust and furniture covered in white cloth, like corpses awaiting burial.

"Who weeps?" he called out. The crying stopped at once.

The next morning, Chen questioned the head servant, Old Wu. The man's face went pale as uncooked dough.

"The western wing has been sealed for three years, Honored Magistrate. Since... since the previous magistrate's third wife died."

"How did she die?"

Old Wu trembled. "She... she drowned herself in the garden pond. On the seventh day of the seventh month. They say she discovered her husband had falsely convicted her father of treason. The old man died in prison before she could prove his innocence."

Chen felt ice in his veins but kept his expression stern. "Superstitious nonsense. Have the western wing cleaned and aired out immediately."

But that night, the crying came again. And this time, Chen saw wet footprints in the corridor, leading from the garden pond to the western wing. They were delicate, a woman's feet, and they glistened in his lantern light before fading like morning dew.

On the third night, Chen decided to wait in the western wing itself. He sat in meditation position, surrounded by candles, the Heart Sutra on his lips. At the hour of the rat, the temperature plummeted. The candles flickered and died one by one. In the darkness, he heard the rustle of silk robes and smelled lotus flowers—but lotus flowers in decay, sweet and rotting.

"Why do you disturb my rest?" he demanded.

A figure materialized before him, translucent as rice paper held to light. She had been beautiful once—high cheekbones, elegant brows—but her robes dripped endlessly with pond water, and her eyes were holes of darkness.

"Justice," she whispered, and her voice was the sound of water filling lungs. "My father died innocent. My husband knew this and let him rot. Now I wait... I wait for justice."

"I am not your husband," Chen said, though his teeth chattered. "Why haunt me?"

Her hollow eyes fixed on his. "Are you not? You who wear his robes, sit in his chair, hold his seals of office? You who would live in this house built on lies and blood?" She drifted closer, and where her feet touched the floor, water pooled. "Prove you are different. Prove you are just."

"How?" The word escaped before Chen could stop it.

She smiled then, a terrible expression on those waterlogged features. "In the archives beneath the eastern pavilion, hidden behind the statue of the God of Literature, you will find a secret compartment. There lies the evidence my husband concealed—proof of my father's innocence, and of the real traitor's identity."

Chen found himself nodding. "If I reveal this truth?"

"Then I shall trouble you no more." She began to fade. "But if you fail... if you choose comfort over justice as he did... then you shall join me in the pond, Magistrate Chen. And your cries shall mingle with mine for all eternity."

The candles reignited suddenly, and Chen found himself alone, sitting in a puddle of foul-smelling water.

He did not sleep that night. At dawn, he went to the archives and found, exactly as the spirit had said, a hidden compartment. Inside were documents that revealed a web of corruption—the previous magistrate had conspired with a merchant guild to frame innocent men and seize their properties. The third wife's father had been only one victim among many.

Chen's hands shook as he read. Exposing this would implicate several powerful families. It would make enemies. It would perhaps end his career, even his life.

That night, he sat again in the western wing, waiting. She came at the same hour, dripping and pale.

"I have read the documents," he said.

"And what will you do?"

Chen met those dark, empty eyes. "Tomorrow, I file the report with the provincial governor. Justice will be done, whatever the cost to myself."

For the first time, her expression softened. The water stopped dripping from her robes. "You are not like him," she whispered. "You are a true magistrate."

"What is your name?" Chen asked. "So that I might have prayers said for your soul."

"Liu Mingzhu," she said, and as she spoke, her form began to change. The water faded away. Color returned to her cheeks. She looked as she must have in life—young, beautiful, with eyes full of intelligence and sorrow. "Thank you, Magistrate Chen. May your righteousness be rewarded."

She bowed deeply, a lady's perfect courtesy, and dissolved into points of light like stars reflecting on still water.

The next day, Chen sent his report. The revelations shook the prefecture. Several officials were arrested. The merchant guild was disbanded. Properties were returned to the families of the wrongly accused. And Chen, despite predictions, was not punished but promoted for his integrity.

He lived in the mansion for thirty more years, serving with distinction. The western wing was opened and turned into a library. The garden pond was cleaned and filled with golden carp and white lotus flowers that bloomed magnificently each summer.

And never again did anyone hear crying in the night.

But sometimes, on the anniversary of Liu Mingzhu's death—the seventh day of the seventh month—servants would find fresh lotus flowers on the shrine Chen had erected in her memory. The flowers were always perfect, dewdrops on their petals catching the morning light like tears of joy.
